Empirical Research Plan: “Physician Workforce, Medicare Spending, and Quality of Care, 1995-2000”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Chosen method: Two–stage least-squares (2SLS) panel-IV with region and year fixed effects, complemented by an event-study robustness exercise around the opening/closing of nearby medical schools.

Why IV?  
• Changes in the local stock of physicians are plausibly endogenous to local demand (reverse causality) and to unobserved region-specific shocks (e.g., epidemics, hospital entry).  
• We exploit quasi-exogenous shocks to physician supply that arise from (i) national cohort-wide entry/retirement patterns and (ii) the 1997 Balanced Budget Act (BBA) cap on Medicare-funded residency slots.  
• A shift–share (“Bartik”) instrument—interacting each region’s pre-period (1995) physician composition with national time-series shocks—generates strong first-stage variation that is plausibly unrelated to contemporaneous local demand shocks after controlling for fixed effects.

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Continuous: Physicians_per1000_rt  = # of active physicians in region r and year t per 1,000 Medicare beneficiaries.  
We will further split the stock into:  
  – PC_Phys_rt  = primary-care physicians per 1,000 beneficiaries  
  – Spec_Phys_rt = specialist physicians per 1,000 beneficiaries

Control/counterfactual  
Other regions in the same year serve as the counterfactual; identification comes from differential predicted shocks generated by heterogeneous baseline shares.

First-stage instrument  
Bartik_IV_rt = Σ_s (Share_rs,1995) × (ΔNatPhys_s,t)  
where s ∈ {age-cohort, specialty, foreign-trained, residency-dependent}. ΔNatPhys_s,t is the national growth rate of group s between t–1 and t, capturing (i) national retirement waves and (ii) the BBA residency cap that differentially constrained specialties reliant on Medicare-funded slots.

Timing  
Panel years 1995–2000. Both the BBA shock (effective 1998) and national retirement bulge (late 1990s) provide time variation; baseline shares are fixed as of 1995.

Event-study robustness  
For the subset of regions within 50 miles of new medical schools opening 1996–1999 (treatment) vs. matched regions (control), we will estimate dynamic effects (-3…+3 years) to visualize pre-trends.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1 (Relevance) – Bartik_IV strongly predicts changes in physician supply. Highly plausible: national retirements and the BBA residency cap created sizeable, specialty-specific swings.

A2 (Exclusion) – Conditional on region & year FE and controls, national cohort shocks influence regional Medicare outcomes only through physician supply, not via independent demand channels. Plausible because (i) these shocks originate outside the region, and (ii) their incidence across regions depends on 1995 composition, which predates the sample period.

A3 (Parallel Trends for event study) – Absent new-school entry, outcomes in treated and control regions would have moved in parallel. We will test using pre-treatment coefficients.

A4 (SUTVA/No spillovers) – National shocks do not differentially affect neighboring regions through migration unrelated to baseline shares. We will cluster by commuting zone and test for spatial spillovers.

A5 (Monotonicity) – Regions with higher baseline reliance on a group s are weakly more affected by national expansions/contractions of s; no “defiers.” Reasonable because supply changes of group s scale proportionally with initial counts.

4. Main Threats and Mitigations  

T1 Selective migration of physicians responding to local spending growth.  
 • Use IV (addresses reverse causality).  
 • Control for lagged spending and demographics; include region×linear trend.

T2 Violation of exclusion: regions with many near-retirement physicians may simultaneously have older, sicker populations.  
 • Add rich controls for beneficiary age-mix, baseline health, income, and hospital capacity.  
 • Placebo: test effect of Bartik_IV on pre-period (1993-94) outcomes.

T3 Measurement error in physician counts (AMA files) attenuates OLS; could bias IV if correlated with baseline shares.  
 • Use multiple sources (AMA masterfile + Medicare provider file); instrument is based on shares, lowering measurement-error correlation.  
 • Errors-in-variables robustness using Simulation-Extrapolation (SIMEX).

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dim IV
library(lmtest)        # coeftest, waldtest
library(sandwich)      # vcovCL

# 1. Load & merge data -----------------------------------------------------
med   <- fread("medicare_region_1995_2000.csv")      # spending, quality, bene counts
phys  <- fread("physician_counts_1995_2000.csv")     # by region x specialty x age
nat   <- fread("national_physician_counts.csv")      # same breakdown, national level

# 2. Construct variables ---------------------------------------------------
# regional physician stocks
phys[, phys_per1000 := phys_total / beneficiaries * 1000]
phys[, pc_per1000   := pc_phys   / beneficiaries * 1000]
phys[, spec_per1000 := spec_phys / beneficiaries * 1000]

# baseline 1995 shares for Bartik
base <- phys[year == 1995, .(share = phys_total / sum(phys_total)), 
             by = .(region, group = interaction(specialty, agecohort))]
setkey(base, region, group)

# national growth shocks
nat[, growth := (phys_total - shift(phys_total)) / shift(phys_total), 
    by = .(group)]

# Bartik instrument
bartik <- merge(base, nat[, .(year, group, growth)], by = "group", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
bartik[, IV := share * growth]
bartik   <- bartik[, .(Bartik_IV = sum(IV, na.rm=TRUE)), by = .(region, year)]

# merge into main panel
panel <- merge(med, phys[, .(region, year, phys_per1000, pc_per1000, spec_per1000)], 
               by = c("region","year"))
panel <- merge(panel, bartik, by = c("region","year"))

# 3. Main specification ----------------------------------------------------
# Outcome 1: log Medicare spending per beneficiary
panel[, lspend := log(spending_per_beneficiary)]

# 2SLS with region & year fixed effects
spec <- feols(lspend ~ pc_per1000 + spec_per1000 | region + year |
              (pc_per1000 + spec_per1000 ~ Bartik_IV), 
              data = panel, cluster = ~region)

summary(spec)

# 4. Robustness: add region-specific trends -------------------------------
spec_trend <- feols(lspend ~ pc_per1000 + spec_per1000 | region + region:year + year |
                    (pc_per1000 + spec_per1000 ~ Bartik_IV),
                    data = panel, cluster = ~region)

# 5. Placebo: pre-period outcome (1993-94) --------------------------------
pre <- panel[year %in% 1993:1994]
placebo <- feols(lspend ~ pc_per1000 | region + year |
                 (pc_per1000 ~ Bartik_IV), data = pre, cluster = ~region)

# 6. Event-study (robustness) using fixest::iplot --------------------------
# define treated==1 if new med school opens in region between 1996-1999
# ... (code omitted for brevity) ...
```

6. Expected Results  

Economic priors:  
• Primary-care supply: – Elasticity around –0.02 to –0.03. A one-unit rise in PC physicians per 1,000 beneficiaries should lower per-beneficiary Medicare spending by roughly 2–3 percent and reduce 30-day AMI mortality by ≈0.1 pp.  
• Specialist supply: + Elasticity around +0.015. More specialists likely raise spending (greater use of procedural care) with ambiguous effects on mortality; may improve procedure-specific outcomes.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  

C1 Relevance (first-stage F > 10): 1  
C2 Exclusion (no direct path): 0.7  
C3 Parallel trends / no differential pre-trends (event-study): 0.8  
C4 No spillovers / SUTVA: 0.6  
C5 Monotonicity (no defiers): 0.9  

Overall, the design is reasonably credible but rests on the exclusion restriction and limited spillovers, which we will probe extensively through robustness and placebo analyses.
